Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial Ends in Mistrial After Juror Deadlock

Lindsay Clancy, a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children in January 2023, faced a jury that could not reach a unanimous verdict. The trial ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked for seven days. Clancy’s defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis, claiming she was not criminally responsible for her actions. Prosecutors maintained she was in control and therefore criminally liable. Clancy, who is paralyzed and in a wheelchair following her alleged suicide attempt after the killings, remains in psychiatric custody at Tewksbury State Hospital. The case has sparked national debate over mental health, the insanity defense, and the legal standards for criminal responsibility.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and FOX News both mention the 11-1 jury split, but the Daily Wire refers to the holdout as a "male juror," while FOX News states the defense attorney referred to the holdout as a "male inside and outside court." The Daily Wire also claims that the prosecution must prove sanity beyond a reasonable doubt, while CBS News and FOX News both note that Massachusetts law places the burden of proof on the prosecution to show criminal responsibility. The Washington Examiner reports that Republicans criticized the jury for not convicting Clancy, while the BBC and Newsweek focus on public reactions and the broader societal implications of the case. The Daily Wire and FOX News both describe the defense’s arguments, but the Daily Wire adds that the defense’s claim about medication interactions was weak, while CBS News and FOX News do not mention this point.

Sources The Daily Wire · Newsweek · FOX News · CBS News · BBC · Washington Examiner

Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber. The floods, triggered by the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet, caused widespread destruction, wiping away villages, bridges, and hydropower dams. At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods, with more than 4,200 remaining missing. Rescue efforts have focused on hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may have survived for over a week due to air pockets. Over 270 people have been rescued so far.

Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel on Friday, nine days after the floods. Officials identified the two men as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor. The rescue at the Trishuli 3A tunnel brought the total number of survivors to three, including a Chinese national rescued on Saturday. At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel. Officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued, with ongoing efforts to locate survivors in other hydropower projects.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that officials believe 46 people are still alive in an underground room at the Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, while the Associated Press states that at least 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels. The Guardian also mentions that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants along the Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers, whereas the Washington Examiner and NPR report different numbers of missing workers. The Associated Press and BBC mention a Chinese national rescued from a hydropower tunnel, while the Guardian and NPR do not specify the nationality of the rescued workers. The Guardian and ABC News report that the death toll is at least 1,252, while the Associated Press and ABC News report a higher death toll of at least 1,300.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · Washington Examiner · Associated Press · BBC

Midterm mail ballots start to go to voters as litigation creates uncertainty

Mail voting for this year’s midterm elections has begun in several states, including North Carolina, amid ongoing legal battles over President Donald Trump’s attempts to limit the practice. Election officials have stated that ballots will be mailed out as expected, despite the uncertainty caused by litigation. Trump has pushed to restrict mail voting, which he has falsely blamed for his 2020 loss, though he himself has voted by mail. The U.S. Supreme Court recently issued a procedural ruling in Trump’s favor, but did not address the merits of the case. Election officials have warned that confusion over the executive order and court fights has already affected some voters, but they have assured that mail voting remains a safe and secure process.

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to lift a block on its new mail ballot rule for the U.S. Postal Service, which requires mail-in ballots to bear Election Mail markings and be sent in automation-compatible envelopes with unique barcodes. The rule, developed under Trump’s executive order, has been temporarily blocked by a federal judge, who argued that it would be too late in the election cycle to implement such changes without causing significant harm and confusion. The Postal Service’s rule has also been challenged by states and civil rights groups, who argue it infringes on states’ rights to administer elections.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that North Carolina is scheduled to become the first state to widely distribute mail ballots, while Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire note that North Carolina is set to distribute ballots Friday. CBS News states that mail ballots will go out to voters in several states in mid-September, with North Carolina mailing its first ballots Friday. Straight Arrow News confirms that North Carolina is set to distribute ballots Friday, regardless of how the lawsuit proceeds. The Daily Wire mentions that states may voluntarily use the Postal Service’s new system, but none have announced plans to do so, while CBS News states that the Postal Service’s rule requires states to include specific design elements on mail ballot envelopes and submit voter information to an online portal.

Sources ABC News · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · CBS News · NPR · Straight Arrow News

Missouri's top court blocks new House map favoring GOP until voters can weigh in

The Missouri Supreme Court has unanimously blocked the state from moving forward with a new House map that favors Republicans in this year's midterm elections, ordering a statewide vote on whether to uphold or reject the new map. The decision marks a rare setback for Republicans in the national redistricting battle, as they fight to hold onto their slim House majority. The court placed the new districts on hold because citizens submitted petition signatures seeking a referendum. The legislation containing the new districts "did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters." As a result, the congressional map adopted after the 2020 census "remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election."

The new districts were used in the August primaries but cannot be used in the November general election. The court ruled that a constitutional provision allowing a referendum on "any act" of the legislature encompasses congressional redistricting. The ruling capped a year of political maneuvering and legal wrangling over the new districts. Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway indicated her office will appeal to the Supreme Court, calling the decision a "full-fledged constitutional crisis."

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Guardian both state that the new districts were used in the August primaries, while The Washington Examiner and Al Jazeera mention that the new map was used in the primaries. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note that the new map would have shifted the House delegation to seven Republicans and one Democrat, while CBS News and The Washington Examiner do not specify the exact number of seats. The Daily Wire attributes the claim about the 7-1 advantage to the court's decision, while CBS News and The Guardian attribute it to the legislature's plan. The Daily Wire also mentions that the case was brought by Richard von Glahn, the executive director of "People Not Politicians," while CBS News and The Guardian do not name the plaintiff.

Sources CBS News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner

United States likely added 65,000 jobs last month, but jobseekers struggle and pay gains are meager

The U.S. Labor Department is expected to report Friday that the American job market bounced back last month from a dismal July, even though jobseekers continue to struggle and pay gains are slight. The August jobs report likely showed that U.S. employers added a net 65,000 jobs last month after they unexpectedly slashed 23,000 in July. The unemployment rate is expected to have ticked up to a still-low 4.2% last month from 4.1% in July. The lingering effects of high interest rates and Trump’s erratic trade policies discouraged companies from hiring in 2025.

The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs in August, an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, still down from its most recent peak of 4.5% last November. Job growth in June and July were both revised up, with June revised to 31,000 jobs and July revised to 21,000 jobs. Economists had predicted gains would be at least 50,000 new jobs. The August jobs report also showed that average hourly earnings rose 10 cents in August, after a minuscule rise in July.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press reports that the August jobs report likely showed 65,000 jobs added, while The Guardian, Christian Science Monitor, Fox Business, Straight Arrow News, and The Daily Wire all report 162,000 jobs added. The Guardian and The Daily Wire attribute the revised July jobs report to a statistical glitch, while the Associated Press does not. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also report that the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, while the Associated Press reports it ticked up to 4.2%. The Christian Science Monitor and Fox Business report that the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, as does Straight Arrow News. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, while the Associated Press reports it ticked up to 4.2%. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, while the Associated Press reports it ticked up to 4.2%. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, while the Associated Press reports it ticked up to 4.2%. The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, while the Associated Press reports it ticked up to 4.2%.

Sources Associated Press · The Guardian · Christian Science Monitor · Fox Business · Straight Arrow News · The Daily Wire

Excavation work on Trump's arch to begin over next 2 weeks: Interior secretary

The Trump administration announced that excavation work for the proposed 250-foot "triumphal arch" will begin over the next two weeks, according to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. The project, located on Columbia Island between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, is part of a broader effort to leave a lasting mark on Washington, D.C. The National Park Service has endorsed the site for the project, though it noted potential adverse effects on historic sightlines. A lawsuit from three veterans and an architectural historian argues that the project lacks congressional authorization, and the Justice Department has moved to dismiss the case.

The National Capital Planning Commission has not yet issued final approval for the construction plan, and the National Park Service has not finalized its historic-preservation review. The administration claims the excavation is part of an archaeological survey, not actual construction, and that the work will not violate a court order requiring 14 days' notice before construction begins. The project is also under aviation review, with the Federal Aviation Administration still studying its impact on nearby airspace.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and FOX News both report that the Justice Department claims the excavation is not actual construction but an archaeological survey. CBS News and The Guardian also mention this, but CBS adds that the National Park Service has acknowledged potential adverse impacts on the landscape. Straight Arrow News and The New York Post do not mention the DOJ's position on the nature of the excavation work. ABC News states that the National Capital Planning Commission has not issued final approval, while Straight Arrow News and The Guardian note that the commission has given preliminary approval. The New York Post and FOX News mention that the National Park Service report noted adverse effects on sightlines, while CBS News and The Guardian provide more detail on the nature of those effects.

Sources ABC News · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · CBS News · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

US diesel prices hit a record high of $5.85 on average as the Iran war disrupts the flow of fuel

Diesel prices in the U.S. reached an all-time high of $5.85 per gallon, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). This surge is attributed to the ongoing war with Iran, which has disrupted global fuel supplies. Higher diesel costs are expected to increase transportation expenses for goods, affecting consumers through higher prices for items like groceries, clothing, and furniture. The situation has also raised concerns about inflation and its impact on everyday costs.

The war has led to increased volatility in oil markets, with the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil transit route, experiencing heightened tensions. This has contributed to higher crude oil prices, which in turn affect diesel costs. The Trump administration has been involved in efforts to secure oil supplies, including a deal with Venezuela, which aims to increase U.S. oil reserves and potentially lower fuel prices in the long term.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and CBS News both report that diesel prices reached $5.85 per gallon, but CBS News adds that this is the highest since the Russia-Ukraine war, while the Associated Press notes it is the first time ever. The Guardian and Axios provide additional context about the impact on farmers and the broader economy, including the role of global refining capacity and the effect on agricultural costs. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention the Trump-Venezuela deal, while the Guardian and Axios highlight the role of the Strait of Hormuz and the impact on global oil supply. The BBC includes details about the U.S.-Israel war with Iran and mentions the role of Venezuela under Trump's administration, which is not explicitly stated in other accounts.

Sources Associated Press · BBC · The Guardian · Axios · The Daily Wire · CBS News

White House website debuts 5 retro arcade video games that promote Trump's agenda

The White House website unveiled a collection of five low-resolution video games on Thursday, each tied to different aspects of President Donald Trump’s agenda. The games, part of a new section called "Arcade," include "Build the Wall," a Tetris-style game that challenges players to stack sections of a border wall while protecting the country from what the game calls the "coming horde." Another game, "Rio Run," resembles the mobile favorite "Snake," with an icon resembling Trump running around gathering potential border crossers. "Supply Line" is a condensed version of the arcade game "Tapper," where players sort food along an assembly line and reject items that don't meet "Make America Healthy Again" standards. Two games take place over the skies of the nation's capital, including "Flappy Bill," where an eagle carries a bill across the National Mall. "Trump Savings Tycoon" allows players to collect money to "Fill your kids' Trump Accounts," a savings program offering $1,000 to every child born during Trump's term.

The White House announced the launch of the arcade on social media with animations parodying Xbox, PlayStation, and Nintendo loading screens. One such post featured the Sega logo turning into "MAGA," as in Trump's "Make America Great Again" slogan. The initiative is part of the administration's effort to engage a younger audience and promote its policies through interactive media.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that "Trump Savings Tycoon" is part of the administration's savings plan offering $1,000 to every child born during Trump's term. Newsweek and Washington Examiner also mention this program, but Newsweek adds that more than six million Trump Accounts had already been requested as of July 6. Mother Jones does not mention the number of accounts requested, instead focusing on the dehumanizing nature of the games. Straight Arrow News and Al Jazeera do not mention the number of accounts requested or the savings program, while Al Jazeera highlights the backlash from critics who argue the games prioritize entertainment over pressing issues like rising costs and the Iran war.

Sources ABC News · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · Mother Jones · Straight Arrow News · Al Jazeera

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Volkswagen’s plan to cut 100,000 jobs by 2030 threatens livelihoods for thousands of workers, exacerbating economic instability.

Volkswagen announces it will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030

Volkswagen has approved plans to cut 100,000 jobs by 2030 as part of a restructuring effort to address financial challenges and competition. The company announced further cuts of 50,000 jobs and a staggered end to production at four German plants between 2031 and 2034. The restructuring includes a cost-cutting plan to reduce positions by 50,000 by 2030, bringing the total job losses to 100,000. The supervisory board acknowledged overcapacity in Europe for producing 500,000 vehicles with no market. The number of car models produced by the VW group will be cut by half. Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across its brands.

Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, described the plan as a “strong signal for the future” and emphasized the need to align workforce levels with economic realities. The plan was approved after a meeting with shareholders, unions, and state representatives. IG Metall, the company’s largest union, stated that concessions were made on both sides to avoid a dangerous escalation of the conflict. The deal includes a stay of execution for four plants threatened with closure in exchange for staff reductions. Blume also mentioned a “three-figure billion sum” investment to enhance the competitiveness of the company’s brands.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian states that Volkswagen will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030, with an additional 50,000 cuts announced this week, and that the total job losses will be the largest restructuring in the global automotive industry. The BBC reports that the 100,000 job cuts are the result of a plan approved in March for 50,000 cuts, with the current approval bringing the total to 100,000. The Guardian mentions that the number of car models produced by the VW group will be slashed by half, while the BBC states that the number of models will be cut by 50% and complexity reduced by 75%. The Guardian also notes that the total job cuts will amount to about 15% of the company’s employees, while the BBC does not specify the percentage. The Guardian mentions that the supervisory board acknowledged overcapacity in Europe for producing 500,000 vehicles with no market, while the BBC does not include this detail.

Sources The Guardian · BBC

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right or right covered this story.

Gloria Steinem, feminist icon, dies at 92

Gloria Steinem, a journalist, activist, and organizer who became the most recognizable face of the U.S. women's movement, died at 92. Steinem resisted being cast as feminism's singular face, but for six decades she carried its ideas into mainstream America across its second and third waves. She made the personal political: an illegal abortion at 22 preceded decades of fighting first to legalize abortion and then to defend that right. Steinem died peacefully, surrounded by people who loved her at her home in New York City, according to a Thursday announcement posted from her and her foundation's Instagram accounts. "Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard," the announcement said.

Steinem first drew national attention as a journalist in 1963 when she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny and exposed the job's low pay and sexist treatment. Soon, she was both chronicling feminism's emerging second wave and organizing within it. She co-founded Ms. magazine, bringing feminist arguments about work, sex, politics, family, and reproductive rights to a mass audience. She also helped found the National Women's Political Caucus. She took her fight to Congress, testifying for the Equal Rights Amendment in 1970, and to the American people, campaigning for its ratification.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire attributes Steinem's normalization of feminism to her appearance and media presence, contrasting her with earlier feminists like Kate Millett, Angela Davis, and Betty Friedan, whom it describes as "angry, cantankerous, and mentally ill." The Daily Wire also claims Steinem said she would have been "stopped there" if she had had a child as a young single woman, a claim not present in other accounts. The Daily Wire attributes this quote to a 2022 interview with Meghan Markle and Vogue magazine. The Slate article mentions Steinem's abortion in 1957 and her doctor's influence, but does not include the claim about having a child. The Axios article notes Steinem's abortion at 22 and her later activism around abortion rights, but does not mention the 2022 quote. The BBC and NPR accounts focus on her early life, activism, and legacy without the specific claims about her personal life or the 2022 interview.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · NPR · Axios · The Dispatch · Slate

Trading food for medicine and crossing the river by zip line are part of life in Nepal flood zone

Survivors in Nepal’s flood-affected areas are facing severe shortages of essential medicines, with some resorting to selling relief food to afford their prescriptions. Suresh Kumar Karanjit, a resident of a relief center in Devighat, Nuwakot district, described the lack of medicine for his heart condition, stating he sold a carton of noodles he received as relief for 400 rupees ($2.60) to buy his regular medication. The floods, triggered by a glacier collapse on Aug. 26, devastated towns and valleys, destroying homes, roads, bridges, and critical infrastructure. Nepal’s disaster chief, Dharam Raj Uprety, noted that health camps with doctors and medicine have been set up at each relief center, while authorities are also focusing on hygiene and sanitation to prevent disease.

Rescue efforts have focused on hydropower tunnels where workers are believed to have survived for over a week. Two workers were rescued alive from the Trishuli 3A tunnel nine days after the disaster, with one, Sanjay Shah, describing his ordeal of trying to save others before being trapped. Officials confirmed the rescue of Sanjay Shah and Kabir Maharjan, with Maharjan in critical condition. Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina expressed hope that more workers will be rescued. The death toll has risen to at least 1,259, with over 5,000 people missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and Washington Examiner both report that at least 1,259 people were killed, while Al Jazeera and ABC News state the death toll is at least 1,287. The Guardian and ABC News mention 1,287 deaths, with the Guardian also noting that 5,000 people remain missing. The Washington Examiner and Associated Press report that China said 21 people were killed and 541 missing on the Tibet side, while Al Jazeera and ABC News state that China reported 16 additional deaths and 546 missing people, bringing the total to 1,268 and 4,762 missing on both sides. The Guardian and ABC News also mention that more than 5,000 people remain missing, while the Associated Press and Washington Examiner report over 5,000 missing.

Sources Associated Press · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian · ABC News · Washington Examiner

Iran fires on its Gulf neighbors, retaliating for U.S. strikes after a monthlong lull

Iran launched missile and drone attacks on U.S. allies in the Gulf on Wednesday, following a night of American bombardment that included a strike on a wedding party in southern Iran. The six-month conflict has led to rising oil prices and economic instability. The U.S. military struck Iranian military targets, including air defense sites and maritime assets, in response to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and American forces in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials claimed the U.S. strike killed four people, including two children, at a wedding in Kuhestak, while the U.S. denied targeting civilians. The strikes marked the end of a monthlong lull in fighting.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and BBC both report that the U.S. strike killed four people, including two children, at a wedding in Kuhestak. Al Jazeera and BBC also mention that the attack may constitute a war crime. NPR and Christian Science Monitor report that the U.S. strike hit a home hosting a wedding, while BBC and Al Jazeera specify that the attack occurred at a home in Kuhestak. Christian Science Monitor and FOX News mention that the U.S. strike targeted Iranian military assets, including mine-laying capabilities and communications sites, while NPR and BBC do not specify these targets. FOX News and Straight Arrow News report that the conflict began on February 28, 2026, with Operation Epic Fury, while other accounts do not mention this date or operation.

Sources NPR · BBC · Al Jazeera · Christian Science Monitor · Straight Arrow News · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump names new acting Army secretary after Driscoll resigns

President Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle, a civilian leader in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, as the acting Army secretary, following the resignation of Dan Driscoll earlier this week. Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the Army for civil works. Driscoll resigned as the Army's top civilian leader this week, following months of behind-the-scenes friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Driscoll had drawn up plans to transform the Army's operations but shared concerns with the Trump administration that Hegseth had pushed out some of the generals responsible for implementing those plans.

Telle will now oversee the nation's largest fighting force at a time when the U.S. is still engaged in conflict with Iran and significant Army forces are stationed in the Middle East. The war has contributed to the U.S. military's shortfall in critical weapons like the Patriot and THAAD defense missile interceptor systems, which are operated by the Army. Democrats and Republicans lamented Driscoll's departure, with some blaming Hegseth directly. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is retiring and sometimes has clashed with Trump, said on social media that Hegseth "is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks."

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that Driscoll resigned after months of friction with Hegseth and that Hegseth asked Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George to step down in April. FOX News and Al Jazeera also mention the tensions between Hegseth and Driscoll, but FOX News adds that Tillis called for Trump to replace Hegseth, while Al Jazeera highlights Hegseth's broader controversies, including the "Signalgate" incident. The Guardian and CBS News note that Driscoll did not provide a reason for his resignation, while Newsweek states Driscoll gave no explanation for his departure. CBS News and The Guardian mention that Driscoll was an ally of Vice President JD Vance, while FOX News and Al Jazeera attribute Tillis's criticism of Hegseth to his own political stance.

Sources CBS News · Newsweek · FOX News · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian

Russia’s strikes near Moldova raise alarm over Putin’s plans for Europe’s eastern flank

Russia has intensified strikes against Ukrainian-Moldovan border infrastructure, according to Moldova’s national security advisor Stanislav Secrieru, who told Fox News Digital. These strikes are aimed at disrupting Ukraine’s grain exports through Moldova, which has become a key transit route for Ukrainian grain to Romanian ports. Moldova cut rail transit tariffs by half to maintain the flow of exports. The Moldovan government has also reported multiple violations of its airspace by Russian drones and missiles, with 17 incidents recorded in August 2025. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently visited Moldova to express solidarity with President Maia Sandu amid the escalating tensions.

The European Union and NATO have responded to recent Russian actions, including a suspected drone attack on a cargo plane in Germany’s Leipzig airport. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and called for a stronger response. Germany has blamed Russia for the attack and announced sanctions, including the closure of Russian cultural institutions, which Russia has retaliated by closing its own Goethe-Institut centers in Russia.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Moldova has recorded 17 Russian airspace violations in August 2025, while the Christian Science Monitor and The Guardian do not mention specific numbers of violations. The Guardian and BBC attribute the Leipzig drone attack to Russia, while the BBC adds details about the suspects identified in the attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport and another with Latvian and Russian passports. The Guardian also notes that the attack was linked to Russia’s hybrid warfare tactics, a point not explicitly made in the other accounts. The Christian Science Monitor mentions that Russia is suspected of paying local gangs to carry out sabotage, a claim not made by the other outlets.

Sources FOX News · BBC · Christian Science Monitor · The Guardian · NPR · ABC News

Biden-appointed judge blocks Trump’s latest birthright citizenship executive order

A federal judge has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship, citing the Supreme Court’s prior ruling that children born in the U.S. to parents who are unlawfully present are citizens at birth. The order, issued in August 2026, sought to deny automatic citizenship to children of “alien enemies” and those engaged in “birth tourism.” Judge Deborah Boardman, a Biden appointee, issued a preliminary injunction against the executive order, arguing it was “almost certainly unconstitutional” as it contradicted the Supreme Court’s decision in *Barbara v. Trump*. The White House criticized the ruling, calling it an example of “activist judges” attempting to block Trump’s “commonsense agenda.”

The executive order aimed to limit birthright citizenship for children of foreign government employees and those whose parents are deemed “alien enemies,” including members of designated terrorist organizations. The order also targeted “birth tourism,” the practice of traveling to the U.S. to give birth for citizenship. The Supreme Court had previously ruled that children of undocumented immigrants and temporary visitors are citizens at birth, but allowed for exceptions such as foreign diplomats and during hostile occupations.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the judge cited the Supreme Court’s June ruling in *Barbara v. Trump* and that the White House called the ruling an “activist judge appointed by Biden attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda.” The New York Post states that the judge cited the same ruling and that the White House spokesperson said the order was “consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court.” The Federalist adds that the judge previously gave a lenient sentence to the attempted killer of Justice Kavanaugh and that Rep. Chip Roy introduced impeachment articles against her. The Guardian and BBC both note that the judge cited the Supreme Court’s June ruling and that the government has not yet issued guidelines on how to implement the restrictions. Straight Arrow News mentions that the judge initially denied an injunction due to the complaint referencing the 2025 order, which had already been struck down.

Sources FOX News · New York Post · The Federalist · The Guardian · BBC · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

ICE officer faces federal charges for lying over shooting of Venezuelan immigrant

Federal prosecutors have charged an ICE officer, Christian Castro, with making false statements to investigators about the shooting of a Venezuelan immigrant, Julio Sosa-Celis, in Minnesota in January. The charges are part of a broader investigation into the incident, which occurred during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Minneapolis known as Operation Metro Surge. Castro was initially accused of shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg through a closed door, but surveillance footage contradicted his account of the incident. The Justice Department initially charged Sosa-Celis with assault, but later dropped those charges after acknowledging that officers involved made untruthful statements. Castro is also facing state-level assault charges in Minnesota.

The shooting has sparked controversy, with Sosa-Celis's attorney criticizing the federal charges as insufficient, arguing that Castro lied to cover up the shooting without self-defense justification. Minnesota officials have sought to extradite Castro from Texas, but Texas Governor Greg Abbott refused to sign the extradition request, citing Castro's return to Texas for work. A federal judge ruled against Minnesota's request to keep Castro in jail pending extradition, allowing him to be released.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both report that the Justice Department initially charged Sosa-Celis with assault, which was later dropped after acknowledging untruthful statements by officers. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention that the charges against Sosa-Celis were dismissed with prejudice in February, citing newly discovered evidence. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian note that the federal charges against Castro were blocked by Justice Department officials, while NPR and The Daily Wire state that the federal charges are separate from the state charges. The Guardian and BBC mention that the Trump administration launched Operation Metro Surge in early December 2025, while NPR and CBS News refer to it as occurring earlier in the year.

Sources NPR · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · BBC · The Daily Wire · CBS News

Trump asks Supreme Court to lift block on USPS plan to restrict mail voting

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to lift a block on the U.S. Postal Service plan to restrict mail-in voting for the midterm election. Key parts of the plan are currently blocked by a temporary restraining order from a federal judge in Boston. North Carolina is scheduled to start mailing out absentee ballots on Friday, which officially kicks off the voting season for this year's midterms. Election officials have stated that ballots will be mailed out as expected, and they are prepared to administer a secure election even if the new limits go forward.

The USPS plan requires states to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service through an online portal and include specific design elements on mail ballot envelopes, such as barcodes. The plan was issued in response to a March executive order by President Trump, who claimed it was to stop illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens. However, many studies and audits show that such voting is rare. The Supreme Court previously ruled on a procedural question about one of the lawsuits but has not yet ruled on the legality of the order or the USPS plan.

Where the accounts differ

NPR states that the USPS plan has not directly changed mail-in voting for the midterms and that key parts are blocked by a court order. ABC News reports that the USPS plan includes requirements for states to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service through an online portal and that the plan has been held up by multiple lawsuits. CBS News adds that election officials warn the new requirements would be difficult, if not impossible, to implement in time for the midterms. Straight Arrow News mentions that the Supreme Court ruled a lawsuit against the order was filed prematurely and that the Postal Service posted changes to its website, leading to a new lawsuit. Washington Examiner notes that the Supreme Court lifted a lower court order blocking an executive order instructing federal agencies to develop policies regarding mail ballots. Just The News states that the Supreme Court previously ruled the administration could move forward with the executive order but did not rule on its legality.

Sources NPR · ABC News · CBS News · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

U.S. and Venezuela Reach Oil Agreement with U.S. Gaining Control of 65 Billion Barrels

The Trump administration announced a deal granting the U.S. majority control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves, with the U.S. government acquiring a 35% equity stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a private oil company led by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt López. Under the agreement, the U.S. will have the right to purchase 20% of the oil produced by NABEP at the cost of production, while the remaining 80% can be sold to other buyers. The deal also gives the U.S. government veto power over NABEP’s board of directors, requiring a majority of board members to be U.S. citizens. Venezuela’s interim government granted NABEP 100-year rights over 17 oil fields, and the U.S. plans to use the oil to refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has reached historically low levels. Venezuela’s president, Delcy Rodríguez, publicly supported the deal, claiming it could generate over $200 billion in tax revenue for the country.

Chevron announced a separate $7 billion investment to expand its oil production in Venezuela, aiming to increase output to 600,000 barrels per day by 2031. The company has been granted access to two additional oil fields in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt, which contains vast reserves of extra-heavy crude. Chevron’s CEO, Mike Wirth, stated the investment reflects confidence in Venezuela’s resource potential and its ability to attract investment. The deal with NABEP is part of a broader U.S. strategy to boost oil production and lower gas prices, with Trump claiming the agreement would “substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future.”

Where the accounts differ

Fox Business reports that the U.S. government received a 35% ownership stake in NABEP’s parent company through the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital, while The Guardian and Axios describe the same stake as being held by the Pentagon. The Daily Wire states that Chevron’s investment is part of the broader agreement with NABEP, while CBS News and Axios note that Chevron’s investment is separate from the Trump administration’s deal with NABEP. The Guardian and Axios mention that Betancourt has been investigated by U.S., Swiss, and Spanish authorities over alleged money laundering, while Fox Business and The Daily Wire provide more detail on the nature of the investigations and Betancourt’s denial of wrongdoing. The Daily Wire and Axios report that Betancourt was listed as an unnamed “conspirator” in a 2018 federal indictment, while Fox Business and The Guardian do not mention this specific charge.

Sources Fox Business · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News · Axios · Straight Arrow News

Two dead and three officers injured in Minneapolis shooting

A shooting occurred in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday, resulting in two fatalities and three injured police officers. The suspect was killed, according to multiple outlets. The incident took place near 15 E. Grant St., specifically at Loring Towers, a high-rise apartment building. Officers were involved in a prolonged response, including the use of long guns and armored vehicles. Several individuals were taken to the hospital, with at least one person dying at the scene. The Minnesota governor and other officials expressed support for law enforcement and condolences for the victims.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News differ on the number of fatalities, with the Examiner reporting two dead and FOX News stating three. The Washington Examiner and Newsweek also differ on the number of injured, with the Examiner reporting at least five others injured and Newsweek stating five others wounded. The Daily Wire and CBS News both report that the suspect died, but the Daily Wire mentions that the suspect's death was reported as suicide, while CBS News states it was a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The FOX News and Just The News differ on the number of injured officers, with FOX News reporting four others injured and Just The News stating three officers were injured. The Newsweek account provides additional details about the suspect, Carlton Johnson II, including his eviction status and alleged threats, which are not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · CBS News · FOX News · Just The News · Newsweek

Lindsay Clancy's murder trial deadlocked after five days of deliberations

Lindsay Clancy, 36, faces three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, found strangled at their home in January 2023. A jury of nine women and three men has been deliberating for five days, with jurors reporting they remain deadlocked. Judge William Sullivan gave them a Tuey-Rodriguez charge to continue deliberations. Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, citing postpartum psychosis. Her defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, said she is emotionally unable to handle another trial. A woman, Dawn Light, 56, was arrested for allegedly filming jurors outside the courthouse, though she claims she was only trying to take a photo of Clancy.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that retired judge Jack Lu claims social media has shifted the conventional wisdom about retrials, favoring the defense now due to its influence. The Daily Wire characterizes the jurors as part of a "deranged TikTok mob" and criticizes the defense's narrative as a "mass psychosis" rooted in "narcissism" and "feminism." The Federalist references historical cases like Constance Fisher's drownings in the 1950s and ties the current case to "feminist victimhood dogma" and "therapeutic culture." The Guardian and BBC both report on Dawn Light's arrest for filming jurors, with the Guardian noting the judge's order prohibiting such actions. The New York Post adds that Light was arrested around 3:40 p.m. and that the jury requested dismissal at 3:30 p.m. on Tuesday.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Federalist · The Guardian · BBC · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

USS Lincoln crew hits the streets of Thai beach city after lengthy Middle East deployment

The USS Abraham Lincoln, a U.S. aircraft carrier, arrived in Pattaya, Thailand, after a record-setting deployment to the Middle East. The ship, which has been at sea for over 260 days, is expected to stay in Thailand for several days before continuing its journey back to the U.S. Crew members disembarked at Laem Chabang port, with some heading to Pattaya, a popular destination for U.S. troops. Vendors and travel agents gathered near the Hard Rock Hotel, offering souvenirs and services to the arriving sailors. The ship’s deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 260 days, with the total deployment lasting 286 days. The Navy has acknowledged concerns about mental health and food shortages but has downplayed the severity of the issues.

The Lincoln’s arrival in Thailand has drawn attention due to its long deployment and the potential impact on the local economy. Pattaya, a city known for its nightlife and tourism, has increased security measures around the area. Local officials estimate the visit could bring in around $3 million for the tourism-dependent city. The ship’s stop is part of a larger U.S. military operation in the Middle East, with the Lincoln having been diverted from its original Pacific route due to the war with Iran. The ship is expected to depart Thailand this weekend.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and The Guardian differ on the exact duration of the Lincoln’s uninterrupted time at sea, with AP reporting 264 days and The Guardian stating 270 days. The Guardian also mentions reports of attempted suicides on the ship, which the Associated Press does not include. The Daily Wire and Newsweek both report that the Lincoln has spent over 260 days at sea, but Newsweek adds that the deployment has prompted calls for investigations into deteriorating conditions and mental health concerns. The Guardian and BBC differ on the exact number of days at sea, with the Guardian stating 270 days and the BBC reporting 250 days. The Daily Wire and The Guardian both mention the presence of sex workers in Pattaya, but the Guardian provides more context about the city’s history with U.S. troops and its transformation into a nightlife hub.

Sources Associated Press · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian · Newsweek · BBC · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Apple changes name of Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ in maps app

Apple has updated the label for Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in its maps app for U.S. users, following an executive order from President Donald Trump. The change occurred on Tuesday, the same day John Ternus became Apple’s new CEO. Apple is now the second U.S.-based tech giant to comply with Trump’s order, following Google, which also changed the name for U.S. users. The U.S. Geographic Names Information System, which standardizes federal naming conventions, was cited by both companies as the basis for the change. Canadian users continue to see “Lake Ontario,” while international users may see both names. MapQuest, another map provider, has refused to change the name, stating it will not comply with Trump’s request.

The renaming of Lake Ontario is part of Trump’s broader effort to assert U.S. influence over naming conventions, including renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” and changing the name of Denali to “Mount McKinley.” Trump’s order does not compel private companies to change their naming conventions, but it does update the U.S. government’s official reference guide. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum stated that Trump “reached out to Apple directly” to request the change, though Apple did not immediately comment on the matter.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both state that Trump “reached out to Apple directly” to request the name change, while Axios and Just The News attribute the claim to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. Al Jazeera and The Guardian mention that Trump’s order does not compel private companies to change their naming conventions, whereas Axios and The Guardian also note that Trump’s order does not compel Canada to change the name. The Guardian and Axios clarify that Canadian officials have stated they will not call Lake Ontario “Lake America,” while Al Jazeera and The Guardian do not explicitly state this.

Sources Al Jazeera · Axios · BBC · Just The News · The Guardian

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump to speak on both nights of midterm convention in programming shuffle: Report

President Donald Trump is now scheduled to speak on both nights of the Republican Party’s 2026 midterm convention next week, according to a report. The event in Dallas is set to mark the first midterm convention of its kind, highlighting the administration’s crackdown on fraud, tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and increased access to healthcare through TrumpRx. The convention’s opening night will coincide with a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. On Thursday night, the convention is set again to compete with viewers due to an NFL rivalry matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, Australia. Several major networks, including CBS and CNN, are not expected to cover a majority of the two-day convention live starting Sept. 9 in Dallas.

President Trump vowed Wednesday to campaign for Republicans in 35 competitive races during the final month before the midterm elections. He promised to hold telephone town halls in support of embattled candidates, saying that they “work amazingly.” Trump specifically noted that he will be campaigning on behalf of congressional candidates, but not gubernatorial ones. He also pledged to travel to Texas to campaign for Senate candidate Ken Paxton, before joking: “You might not like the way he dresses.” Trump also plans to travel to Alaska and stump for GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The New York Post both report that Trump will speak on both nights of the convention, while The Daily Wire and Newsweek focus on Trump’s campaign strategy for the midterms. The Washington Examiner mentions the convention’s opening night coinciding with a Super Bowl rematch, while The New York Post and Newsweek do not. The Daily Wire and The New York Post both report that Trump will campaign in 35 races, while The Washington Examiner and Newsweek do not mention the number of races. The Daily Wire and The New York Post both report that Trump will hold telephone town halls, while The Washington Examiner and Newsweek do not. The Daily Wire and The New York Post both report that Trump will campaign in Texas for Ken Paxton, while The Washington Examiner and Newsweek do not.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · CBS News · New York Post · Newsweek · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

NBA suspends Clippers owner Ballmer, fines team $30M, Kawhi Leonard $700K in cap circumvention case

The NBA announced on Wednesday that Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer has been suspended for one year and the team fined $30 million for violating salary cap circumvention rules. Kawhi Leonard was fined $700,000 for his role in the case. The league cited the Clippers for improperly funneling off-court endorsement and income opportunities to Leonard through corporate partners, including Aspiration, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics, and Lockton Insurance. The investigation, which began in September 2025, was prompted by a report from podcast journalist Pablo Torre about a $28 million endorsement contract between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC, a company that filed for bankruptcy last year. The Clippers had previously denied wrongdoing and stated they would challenge the findings. Leonard, through his new agent, expressed regret for the distraction caused by the situation and accepted responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within his inner circle.

The NBA also suspended President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank for six months and team president of business operations Gillian Zucker for one year. The league accused Ballmer of failing to create conditions under which his organization abided by the NBA’s circumvention rules. Leonard’s trade to the Toronto Raptors, which had been on hold pending the investigation, is now expected to proceed, with both teams indicating they are moving forward with the deal.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both mention that the Clippers had said they would challenge the findings, while BBC and Al Jazeera include the Clippers’ statement about the investigation being "heavily biased" and "predetermined narrative." The Guardian and Al Jazeera note that the investigation was conducted by Wachtell Lipton, a New York law firm, while NPR and BBC do not specify the law firm. The Guardian and Al Jazeera also mention that the NBA’s investigation found a "pattern of misconduct" and that the Clippers were a "prior offender" of salary cap circumvention rules, which are not explicitly stated in NPR, Newsweek, or BBC. Just The News does not mention the investigation being conducted by a law firm or the Clippers being a prior offender.

Sources NPR · Newsweek · Just The News · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · BBC

No source labeled right covered this story.

Warnings Over Coast Guard Jet Surfaced Before Mullin Emergency Landing

A Coast Guard plane carrying Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin made an emergency landing after losing an engine on Wednesday. The C-37A aircraft, a military version of a Gulfstream V, landed safely at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport with 14 people on board and no injuries reported. Mullin confirmed the landing on X, stating the pilots handled the situation "feel routine" with "no panic, just straight professionalism." The pilot reported losing the right engine and requested an emergency landing, according to an audio recording. The incident occurred as the plane was traveling from Georgia to Washington, D.C.

Prior concerns about the aircraft's age were raised by the Department of Homeland Security, which flagged the plane for obsolescence issues. In 2025, DHS stated the C-37A was "22 years old and faces significant avionics and communications obsolescence issues," which could impact its availability for critical missions. The plane is one of two long-range command and control aircraft used by the Coast Guard to transport senior officials, including the DHS secretary.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek and The Daily Wire both mention the C-37A is the military version of a Gulfstream V, while FOX News and New York Post refer to it as a C101. The Daily Wire and Newsweek state the plane entered Coast Guard service in 2002, while FOX News and New York Post do not specify the service entry date. The Daily Wire and Newsweek note the plane was flagged for obsolescence in 2025, while FOX News and New York Post refer to it as being flagged "last year." The Daily Wire and Newsweek mention the plane was 22 years old, while New York Post and FOX News refer to it as 23 years old. The Daily Wire and Newsweek attribute the obsolescence concerns to DHS, while FOX News and New York Post attribute it to the Coast Guard.

Sources Newsweek · Just The News · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Dan Driscoll Resigns, Leaving Army Without Confirmed Leadership

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submitted his resignation to President Donald Trump, according to multiple outlets. The resignation is pending acceptance by the White House. Driscoll, who became the youngest Army secretary in 2025, has been at the center of tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has dismissed several top military officers. Driscoll’s resignation leaves the Army without Senate-confirmed leadership, as the Senate has not confirmed a new secretary. Under Secretary of the Army Mike Obadal is next in line to serve until a new secretary is confirmed.

Driscoll’s resignation comes amid ongoing turmoil at the Pentagon under Hegseth, who has faced criticism for his management style and the removal of senior military leaders. The Army secretary manages the Army’s budget and long-term planning but does not command troops in the field. Driscoll is close to Vice President JD Vance, and there were prior speculations that he might join Vance’s presidential campaign. The White House has praised Driscoll for his work advancing Trump’s agenda, though the exact nature of his contributions remains unclear.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Caller and FOX News both report that Driscoll submitted his resignation to Trump, but only FOX News attributes the claim to a senior U.S. official. The Daily Wire and ABC News mention Driscoll’s resignation followed a strained relationship with Hegseth and repeated warnings to the White House about Hegseth’s firing of senior officers. CBS News and The Daily Wire note that Driscoll expressed concerns about Hegseth’s impact on Army transformation and readiness. NPR does not mention Driscoll’s concerns about Hegseth’s actions, instead focusing on his relationship with Vance and the broader context of the Iran war.

Sources The Daily Caller · NPR · CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Wire · ABC News

Iran, US exchange new attacks: Who was hit in latest strikes?

The United States and Iran have exchanged a new round of attacks, with the US targeting Iranian military sites and Iran retaliating with missile and drone strikes. The US Central Command confirmed strikes on Iranian military targets along the southern coast, while Iran claimed US attacks hit a wedding in Kuhestak, killing at least four people. Iran also fired ballistic missiles towards Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq’s Kurdish region. US President Donald Trump warned that Iran would be “totally wiped out” if it retaliates. The conflict has raised fears of escalation into a wider regional war.

Iran’s military said it launched attacks on US bases and assets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq’s Erbil. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it hit the Sheikh Isa Airbase in Bahrain and US bases in Jordan and Kuwait. Iran also said it destroyed several US drones and claimed to have killed a number of US soldiers. Kuwait reported intercepting drones and missiles but did not report casualties. Jordanian forces said air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 10 of 13 Iranian ballistic missiles that entered their airspace.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and Washington Examiner both report that Iran claimed a US airstrike hit a wedding in Kuhestak, killing at least four people and wounding 68. The Washington Examiner adds that Iranian officials said at least five people, including a child, were killed. The Daily Caller and UPI do not mention the wedding attack, with UPI instead reporting that the US military struck Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island and Iran retaliated with strikes on US bases in Jordan. The Associated Press and Christian Science Monitor do not mention the wedding attack, focusing instead on the broader conflict and its economic impact.

Sources Al Jazeera · UPI · Associated Press · Christian Science Monitor · Washington Examiner · The Daily Caller

Trump Faces Calls To Spend In Texas As Dems Blitz Republicans

In the Texas Senate race, Democrat James Talarico has outspent Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by tens of millions of dollars, prompting some Republicans to seek President Donald Trump’s financial support. Talarico raised about $31.6 million in the latest fundraising quarter compared to Paxton’s $9.3 million. Senator John Kennedy (R-LA) stated that the Senate GOP lacks budgeted funds for Texas and urged Trump to spend $100 to $200 million. Trump claimed he has $850 million in his campaign account and plans to spend it on Republican candidates. MAGA Inc., a PAC aligned with Trump, has over $400 million in the bank. Talarico, who has been backed by out-of-state Democratic donors, faces a race in a historically red state. Meanwhile, in Massachusetts, Democrat Sen. Ed Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in a primary, marking a rare win for older Democratic incumbents. Markey, 80, ran against Moulton, 47, who criticized Markey’s age. The race highlighted internal Democratic debates over generational politics.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Federalist both mention Senator John Kennedy’s call for Trump to spend money in Texas, but The Federalist adds that Kennedy implied Paxton is on his own. The Daily Wire states that MAGA Inc. has over $400 million in the bank, while The Washington Examiner and The Daily Caller do not mention this figure. The Daily Wire and The Federalist both report that Trump has $850 million in his campaign account, but The Federalist adds that the Senate GOP has not committed to spending on Paxton. The Daily Wire and The Washington Examiner both describe Talarico’s past progressive views, but The Washington Examiner provides specific examples from a 2020 Zoom forum, which The Daily Wire does not. The Daily Caller and The Federalist both report Markey’s victory over Moulton, but The Daily Caller adds that Markey defeated Moulton in a landslide, while The Federalist does not specify the margin.

Sources The Daily Wire · FOX News · Slate · Washington Examiner · The Daily Caller · The Federalist

Charlie Kirk Assassination Case Faces Make-Or-Break Court Moment

A Utah judge is expected to decide whether Tyler Robinson will stand trial for the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, and whether prosecutors will be allowed to pursue the death penalty. Following a five-day preliminary hearing, Judge Tony Graf will hear closing arguments from the state and defense for a maximum of two hours each before ultimately giving his ruling. Robinson, 23, is charged with aggravated murder and multiple other felonies in the September 2025 fatal shooting of Kirk at Utah Valley University, where he was engaging others with differing political views. Prosecutors have said they intend to seek the death penalty if Robinson is convicted. Robinson’s attorneys have asked Graf to reject the aggravating circumstance that could make the killing eligible for capital punishment, arguing that prosecutors have not shown the shooter knowingly created a “great risk of death” to anyone other than Kirk. Prosecutors counter that others were indeed at risk when the shot was fired.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and FOX News both report that Robinson surrendered to the Washington County Sheriff’s Office about 33 hours after Kirk was shot, arriving with his parents and a family friend. The Daily Wire states that Robinson’s father had reportedly confronted him after recognizing images of the suspected shooter released by authorities, while FOX News does not mention this detail. The Guardian and CBS News both state that Robinson’s DNA was found on the murder weapon, but the Guardian adds that the DNA testing was questioned by Robinson’s lawyers, while CBS News does not mention this. The Guardian and CBS News both report that prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political views against gay marriage and transgender rights, while FOX News and The Daily Wire do not mention this specific motive. The Guardian and CBS News both state that the judge ruled there is sufficient evidence to try Robinson for aggravated murder, while The Daily Wire and FOX News do not mention this ruling explicitly.

Sources The Daily Wire · NPR · FOX News · The Guardian · CBS News · BBC

Kalshi bans ex-congressman George Santos from prediction platform for life

Kalshi, a prediction market platform, announced on Monday that it has permanently banned former Republican congressman George Santos from its platform. The ban comes after Santos was accused of profiting from bets tied to his own attendance at Donald Trump’s State of the Union address earlier this year. Kalshi imposed a $71,356 fine alongside the lifetime ban, citing Santos’s refusal to cooperate fully with its internal investigation. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) previously fined Santos $17,500 and ordered him to return profits from his trades. Santos responded on X, thanking Kalshi for the ban and mocking the platform’s longevity.

Santos, who was expelled from Congress in December 2023 after being found to have defrauded donors and lied about his finances, pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud and identity theft charges in 2024. He was sentenced to more than seven years in prison but served less than three months before Trump commuted his sentence. In July, Santos agreed to pay $35,000 to settle the CFTC’s case without admitting wrongdoing, which also barred him from trading on any platform for three years. Kalshi’s lifetime ban adds an additional penalty.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC both state that Santos made over $17,500 in profit from his trades, while the Straight Arrow News reports he earned $17,839.57. The Guardian and ABC News mention Santos was fined $71,356 by Kalshi, while the BBC reports the fine as $71,356 (£38,000). The Guardian and NPR note Santos made more than $17,000 in profit, while the Straight Arrow News states he wagered more than $17,000. The Guardian and CBS News report Santos was banned for refusing to cooperate with Kalshi’s investigation, while the Straight Arrow News adds that Santos criticized Kalshi for not following its own notices and deadlines. The Guardian and BBC attribute the $17,500 profit to the CFTC, while the Straight Arrow News attributes it to Kalshi.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · CBS News · BBC · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Police kill knife-wielding woman near Times Square after deadly stabbing

A woman armed with knives stabbed two people in Times Square on Monday, prompting police to shoot and kill her. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani confirmed the incident, stating one victim died and the other was in stable condition. The suspect, identified as Pamela Cisneros, was also killed in the shooting. Both victims and the suspect were taken to Bellevue Hospital. The New York City Police Department described the attack as random and unprovoked, with no terrorism involvement. The shooting occurred near West 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue, just before 4:30 p.m.

The suspect, Pamela Cisneros, 49, of Queens, was identified as the attacker. She stabbed a 68-year-old man and a woman, both of whom were taken to Bellevue Hospital. The woman victim, Erin Piacenti, 32, of Chester, New Jersey, was a Bank of America vice president. The male victim was in stable condition. Police said Cisneros had a history of mental health issues and was emotionally disturbed. The confrontation with officers lasted about four minutes before she was shot after refusing to drop her knives.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both report that the woman was shot after she approached officers with a knife, but The Guardian adds that she told police, “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you.” The Daily Wire and CBS News also include this quote, while FOX News and Fox Business attribute the quote to police commissioner Jessica Tisch. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian differ in the number of victims, with The Examiner stating two victims and one suspect died, while The Guardian and others specify that the woman victim and the suspect died, with the male victim surviving. The Daily Wire and CBS News provide additional details about Erin Piacenti’s employment and personal life, which are not included in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · FOX News · The Daily Wire · CBS News · Fox Business

Lindsay Clancy trial: Jury sent home for the day without a verdict

The jury in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy was sent home on Tuesday after failing to reach a unanimous verdict. The jury, composed of nine women and three men, had been deliberating for over 23 hours across four days. The judge, William Sullivan, instructed them to continue their deliberations. ABC News reported that if the jury remains deadlocked, the judge may declare a mistrial, allowing the case to be retried. The trial has been ongoing since July 20, 2026, and has drawn significant public attention.

The case centers on whether Clancy, 36, acted with premeditation or was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children in 2023. The prosecution argues she made a calculated decision, while the defense claims she was not criminally responsible due to her mental state. The jury is considering several verdict options, including first-degree murder, second-degree murder, and not guilty by reason of insanity. The outcome will determine whether Clancy faces life in prison or psychiatric detention.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that under Massachusetts law, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible, while The Free Press mentions that the insanity defense is treated differently in Massachusetts courts. FOX News states that a retired judge believes a verdict is still possible despite the deadlock, whereas The Federalist focuses on public reaction to the trial rather than the legal process. The New York Post notes that a woman was arrested for allegedly filming jurors, a detail not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources ABC News · BBC · The Free Press · FOX News · The Federalist · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Eight Democrats join Republicans in voting to condemn socialism

The House of Representatives passed a resolution condemning socialism in a 220-192 vote, with two Democrats voting present. The resolution, which includes a condemnation of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), was supported by eight Democrats, including Reps. Jared Golden (D-ME) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-WA). The vote followed a procedural rule vote that passed 210-208, with Golden and Perez defecting from their party to ensure the resolution could move forward. The resolution also includes support for the SAVE America Act, a Republican-backed bill aimed at restricting voting rights. The vote was part of a broader effort by Republicans to frame Democrats as supporting socialist policies, with some Republicans using the vote to highlight perceived failures in Senate leadership.

The resolution was part of a larger procedural package that included other bills, such as the Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act, which Rep. Jared Golden (D-ME) co-authored. The vote was met with criticism from some Democrats, who accused Golden and Perez of betraying their party. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) called the defections a "significant breach of trust" and stated that the Democratic Caucus would address the issue.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and CBS News both report that the resolution passed with a 220-192 vote, but the Washington Examiner notes that the vote included two Democrats voting present, while CBS News states the same. The Free Press and Just The News both mention the 220-192-2 split, with two Democrats voting present. The Axios account does not mention the exact vote count, instead focusing on the procedural vote that allowed the resolution to move forward. The FOX News account does not mention the exact vote count, instead focusing on the procedural vote and the debate over the resolution.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · CBS News · Axios · Just The News · The Free Press

No source labeled left covered this story.

The brief ends here.
