US strikes Iran for first time in over a month

The United States launched strikes at Iran on Sunday afternoon for the first time in over a month. The U.S. military struck Larak Island after observing Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces preparing to deploy sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement from U.S. Central Command. The strikes hit two rocket launchers to protect the commercial shipping lane after the military finished clearing the mines throughout the waterway last week. The strikes mark a return to military action after the Trump administration shifted its focus to economic measures, as the U.S. last struck Iranian missile and drone facilities on July 29.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and UPI both report that the U.S. struck rocket launchers on Larak Island to prevent the IRGC from deploying sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The Washington Examiner attributes the claim that the U.S. cleared the mines in the waterway to Capt. Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command, while UPI attributes the same claim to a statement from CENTCOM. The Straight Arrow News reports that Iran fired missiles at U.S. bases in Jordan after the strike, which the Washington Examiner and UPI do not mention. The Mother Jones article focuses on internal U.S. military concerns about the sustainability of the war, which is not covered in the other accounts. The Al Jazeera and Associated Press accounts focus on the economic impact of the conflict, which is not covered in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · UPI · Mother Jones · Straight Arrow News · Al Jazeera · Associated Press

Saudi Arabia Ends Its LIV Golf Bet

Saudi Arabia has officially withdrawn its investment from LIV Golf, a professional golf tour founded by golfer Tiger Woods. The decision comes after months of speculation about the kingdom's financial involvement in the tour. LIV Golf, which launched in 2021 as a breakaway from the PGA Tour, has faced ongoing challenges including legal battles and financial instability. The withdrawal marks a significant shift in Saudi Arabia's sports investment strategy, which had previously included major investments in football and other sports.

Where the accounts differ

The Dispatch reports that Saudi Arabia has ended its LIV Golf bet, but does not provide specific details about the nature of the investment or the reasons for the withdrawal. The other accounts do not mention Saudi Arabia's involvement in LIV Golf at all. The Guardian, NPR, ABC News, Associated Press, and BBC do not reference Saudi Arabia's financial ties to LIV Golf or its decision to withdraw.

Sources The Dispatch · The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · Associated Press · BBC

Two people dead and nearly 80 rescued after Grand Canyon flash flood

A flash flood struck the Grand Canyon over the weekend, resulting in at least two deaths and the rescue of nearly 80 people. The National Park Service (NPS) confirmed a second death on Monday, with the body of a 46-year-old man recovered near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River. The flood, which occurred in Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch, led to the evacuation of dozens of visitors by helicopter. The NPS warned that heavy rain and thunderstorms were expected to continue, increasing the risk of further debris flows and flash floods. The Transcanyon Waterline, a key pipeline for water supply, suffered damage, prompting emergency water restrictions.

The flood caused significant damage to infrastructure, including the destruction of most footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek. The NPS called on the public to provide information about missing individuals, with some accounts suggesting up to 15 people remain unaccounted for. The National Weather Service (NWS) noted that the region is under flood watches, with additional rain and thunderstorms forecast for the area.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports two deaths and nearly 80 rescued, while UPI and Straight Arrow News mention one death and multiple missing. Al Jazeera and CBS News state one death and about 15 missing. The Guardian and CBS News both mention the recovery of a 46-year-old man’s body, but the Guardian adds that at least one other body has been recovered, while Al Jazeera and CBS News do not specify additional bodies. The Guardian and UPI note damage to the Transcanyon Waterline, with the Guardian stating 40% of the pipeline was damaged, while UPI mentions "approximately 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline was damaged or destroyed." The Guardian and CBS News report the evacuation of 62 people, while Al Jazeera and UPI mention similar numbers. The Guardian and BBC include quotes from hikers describing the event, while other outlets do not.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · CBS News · BBC · UPI · Straight Arrow News

Jury convicts Duane Davis of murder in 1996 Tupac Shakur killing

A Las Vegas jury convicted Duane “Keffe D” Davis of first-degree murder in the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, marking the first time anyone has been held criminally responsible for the rapper’s death. Prosecutors argued Davis orchestrated the drive-by shooting as revenge for an earlier public beating of his nephew, Orlando Anderson, by Shakur and Death Row Records founder Marion “Suge” Knight. Davis, 63, faces life in prison if convicted. The trial, which lasted over a week, centered on Davis’ repeated public admissions of his role in the killing, including in his 2019 memoir “Compton Street Legend.” Prosecutors claimed Davis was the “shot caller” who ordered the attack, while the defense argued his statements were fabrications meant to boost his street credibility and promote his book.

Davis was not charged with firing the shots that killed Shakur, which prosecutors attribute to his nephew Anderson, who was killed in a 1998 shootout. The prosecution emphasized Davis’ gang leadership and his alleged role in organizing the attack, while the defense highlighted the lack of physical evidence placing Davis at the scene. The trial also touched on the broader gang rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and the Mob Piru Bloods, with Davis’ gang allegedly connected to Death Row Records and Shakur’s entourage linked to the rival Bloods.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and Al Jazeera both state that Davis was not charged with firing the shots, while The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that prosecutors never gathered enough evidence to press charges against him for the actual shooting. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also note that Davis was briefly a suspect in the Notorious B.I.G. murder but was later ruled out, a detail omitted by The New York Post and Al Jazeera. The Daily Wire and The Guardian describe Davis as the only living witness from the car that fired shots at Shakur, a claim not made by The New York Post or Al Jazeera. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also mention that Davis’ memoir was used as evidence, while The New York Post and Al Jazeera describe it as a key part of the prosecution’s case but do not explicitly state it was used as evidence.

Sources New York Post · The Guardian · The Daily Wire · Straight Arrow News · NPR · Al Jazeera

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigns from post

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has resigned from his position, according to the White House. The resignation was confirmed by the White House on Monday, with no specific reason provided. Driscoll, a close ally of Vice President JD Vance, had been in the role since February 2025. His departure follows months of reported friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The White House praised Driscoll for advancing President Trump's agenda, including efforts to enhance military readiness and lethality, and for his role in negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.

Driscoll, an Iraq war veteran and former adviser to JD Vance, was also involved in efforts to modernize the Army, including drone capabilities. He was tapped for an unusual diplomatic role in the Russia-Ukraine conflict. His resignation comes amid a series of leadership changes in the military, including the ousting of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George and Gen. Christopher Donahue, the commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and The Guardian both report that Driscoll resisted Hegseth's pressure to fire Col. David Butler, while CBS News and The Daily Wire do not mention Butler at all. The Guardian and Axios note that Driscoll was the youngest Army secretary in U.S. history, a detail absent in CBS News and The Daily Wire. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that Driscoll was a George ally and lamented his departure, while Axios and CBS News also include this detail. FOX News and The Daily Wire both state that Driscoll submitted his resignation to Trump, while Axios and The Guardian report that the resignation remains pending and has not been accepted by the White House.

Sources Axios · NPR · CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

US Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom

The US Supreme Court ruled on Monday that construction of the White House ballroom can proceed, allowing the project to continue despite legal challenges. The 5-4 decision stated that the National Trust for Historic Preservation likely lacks standing to challenge the project. The court did not address the legality of the project itself, focusing instead on the Trust's legal standing. President Trump praised the ruling, calling it a victory and stating the ballroom will be one of the greatest ever built in Washington, D.C. The project, which includes a large underground bunker, is part of a broader effort to renovate the White House and surrounding areas.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation argued that the construction is causing irreversible damage to a historical landmark and that Congress must approve the project. Alison Hoagland, a member of the Trust, claimed that the ballroom would harm her aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests. Chief Justice John Roberts, in his dissent, said the injuries claimed by Hoagland were sufficient to allow the lawsuit to proceed and that the project was likely unlawful. The Trust expressed disappointment with the ruling but welcomed the dissent.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the ballroom is part of a wider effort to transform Washington's cityscape, including the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a planned "Arc de Trump." CBS News mentions the ballroom is 90,000 square feet and that the court did not address the legality of the East Wing project. Axios states the project is estimated to cost at least $600 million, up from an initial $400 million. UPI notes the project is $400 million and that the court did not say if the project was legal. Straight Arrow News mentions the project is 65% complete and that the cost has ballooned to $600 million. Just The News states the ballroom is roughly two-thirds complete and part of Trump's efforts to "beautify" the capital.

Sources BBC · CBS News · Axios · UPI · Straight Arrow News · Just The News

Trump says Venezuelan oil will replenish Strategic Petroleum Reserves

President Donald Trump claimed on Sunday that Venezuelan oil will replenish the United States’s Strategic Petroleum Reserves, calling it a "Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States." Trump attributed the depletion of the reserves to former President Joe Biden, stating that Biden had "virtually emptied" the reserves. The deal, announced on Friday, involves securing majority U.S. control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela. The White House stated that the agreement would help refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has been drawn down due to global oil supply disruptions, including the conflict in Iran.

The White House provided additional details on Monday, revealing that the deal involves a private joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt. The agreement grants the Pentagon a 35 percent ownership stake in the company and guarantees the U.S. a right to purchase 20 percent of the output at cost. Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez granted the company 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels, many of which were previously controlled by Russian or Chinese firms.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and UPI both state that Trump claimed the reserves had been "virtually emptied" by Biden, while CBS News and NPR attribute the depletion to a combination of factors including the release of oil for price stabilization and congressional drawdowns. The Washington Examiner and UPI claim the deal involves "majority U.S. control" of the oil reserves, while the Al Jazeera and NPR accounts describe the agreement as granting the U.S. a 35 percent ownership stake and a right to purchase 20 percent of the output at cost. The Daily Caller provides a detailed timeline of the SPR’s depletion, including specific figures on the number of barrels released and the impact of congressional decisions.

Sources Washington Examiner · Al Jazeera · The Daily Caller · NPR · CBS News · UPI

Russian drone and missile attacks kill at least 12 in Kyiv and surrounding region

Russian forces launched a large aerial assault on Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than a dozen others, including three children, according to Ukrainian officials. The attacks, which occurred overnight into Tuesday, targeted civilian infrastructure and residential buildings, with eight people killed in Kyiv itself and four others in the surrounding region. The strikes marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian attacks on Kyiv, with a sustained barrage of drones and missiles that have increasingly involved fast, jet-powered drones. In the Kyiv region, a strike on a weapons depot killed 38 people, with four still missing, and the site is now under criminal investigation by Ukraine’s intelligence service. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attacks as part of a strategy to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses and undermine civilian morale.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that a drone strike hit an ammunition depot in Myla village, 15 miles outside Kyiv, killing 38 people and injuring four others. It also details the aftermath, including the discovery of missile shells, mines, and cluster munitions on the property of Vira and Serhii, who were in a bunker during the attack. The Guardian does not mention the number of casualties in Kyiv or the broader region, focusing instead on the local impact. NPR and Al Jazeera both report that at least 12 people were killed in the attacks, with Al Jazeera citing 12 killed and 21 wounded, while NPR states 38 people were killed in a separate attack on a weapons depot in the Kyiv region. The Guardian and UPI both mention the attack on the weapons depot, but the Guardian provides more specific details about the location and the aftermath. The BBC and UPI mention the killing of six railway workers in Kyiv, while the Guardian and NPR do not. The Guardian also notes that the death toll rose by one to 38, while other accounts do not specify the exact number of casualties in the Kyiv region.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera · Associated Press · BBC · UPI

U.S. strikes Iran to prevent Hormuz mine threat

The U.S. military struck Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz to prevent the deployment of sea mines, according to a U.S. official. The strike marked the first known U.S. attack on Iran since late July. Iran retaliated by launching ballistic missiles at a U.S. base in Jordan, though no damage or casualties were reported. The Jordanian military intercepted eight missiles. The U.S. Central Command stated the strike was a "limited, precise action" against "minelaying forces posing an imminent threat." Oil prices surged following the strike, with Brent crude up 2.9% and U.S. crude up 2.7%. The Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route, remains closed to commercial traffic, though Iran and Oman agreed on a temporary maritime route.

The conflict has led to significant disruptions in oil trade, with Brent crude rising about 22% since the war began in February. The closure of the strait has affected global oil prices and exposed U.S. energy companies to risks, with some reporting reduced oil and gas supplies from the Gulf region. The U.S. strike is part of a broader military and economic pressure campaign against Iran, which includes sanctions and a naval blockade affecting Iran's oil exports.

Where the accounts differ

AP reports the U.S. strike occurred on the Strait of Hormuz, with oil prices surging 3% following the attack. Al Jazeera states the strike was in response to Iran’s closure of the strait and notes the rise in oil prices since February. Axios and Washington Examiner both mention the U.S. strike on Larak Island and the Iranian retaliation with missiles. BBC and Straight Arrow News report the strike killed two people and injured two others, while Axios and Washington Examiner attribute the strike to U.S. forces observing Iranian preparations for mine deployment. Al Jazeera and BBC provide more context on the economic impact and the role of U.S. energy companies in the region.

Sources Associated Press · Al Jazeera · Axios · BBC · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner

Number of missing in Nepal and Tibet rises to 3,000 as bad weather hampers search

A catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border has left at least 900 people dead and more than 3,000 missing, according to conflicting reports from Nepali and Chinese authorities. The disaster, triggered by a glacial collapse, devastated mountainous regions and caused widespread destruction. Rescue operations have been hampered by poor weather, with aerial rescues temporarily halted and ground teams struggling through mud and debris. Over 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal, with efforts focused on hydropower tunnels where dozens of workers are believed to be trapped. International aid has been pledged, including from the U.S., India, and the EU, to support recovery efforts. Survivors describe losing everything, with many left homeless and without access to clean water or food.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports a combined death toll of 691 with more than 3,000 missing, while UPI and ABC News cite a higher death toll of at least 919. The Guardian states that Nepal’s disaster agency reported 675 dead and 2,498 missing, whereas UPI and ABC News note Nepal’s National Disaster Management Authority reported 903 bodies recovered and 4,247 missing. Al Jazeera and the Guardian mention 933 hydropower workers among the missing, while UPI and ABC News report 933 workers missing but with different numbers of total missing. The Guardian and Al Jazeera note that 517 foreigners are missing, while UPI and ABC News report 592 foreign nationals missing. The Guardian and Al Jazeera state that 261 foreigners are among those missing in Tibet, while UPI and ABC News do not specify the number of foreigners missing in Tibet. The Guardian and Al Jazeera report that Nepal has requested foreign help for specialized tasks but not search and rescue, while UPI and ABC News do not mention this request.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · Newsweek · UPI · NPR · ABC News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

1 dead, around 15 missing after Grand Canyon hit by flash floods

A flash flood struck parts of Grand Canyon National Park over the weekend, resulting in the death of one person and the disappearance of at least 15 others. The National Park Service (NPS) confirmed the body of a 46-year-old man was recovered near Crystal Rapids on the Colorado River. The flood, which occurred on August 29, 2026, led to the evacuation of at least 62 people and caused extensive damage to infrastructure, including the destruction of footbridges over Bright Angel Creek. The NPS is seeking information about individuals who may have been in the affected areas during the flood, including those at Bright Angel Campground, Phantom Ranch, and the North Kaibab Trail.

The National Park Service reported that the flash flood was triggered by a significant amount of rainfall, with about half an inch to an inch of rain falling within half an hour in the area. The flooding also damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a critical pipeline that supplies water to the park, leading to water restrictions and the closure of lodges and hotels within the park. The NPS is urging visitors to stay away from closed areas and is working to account for individuals who may have been in the affected regions.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News states that at least 15 people were still missing, though the figure is subject to change. Washington Examiner reports that the NPS is asking for information about more than 20 individuals who may be missing or unaccounted for. New York Post mentions that the NPS revised the number of missing people from 20 to 15. Straight Arrow News notes that more than 20 had been reported missing earlier, but the number was later adjusted. FOX News highlights the case of Dr. John Giusti, a Texas chiropractor, and his hiking group, who are among those unaccounted for, though the NPS has not publicly identified the individuals.

Sources CBS News · Washington Examiner · Just The News · New York Post · Straight Arrow News · FOX News

Google Maps Complies With Trump’s ‘Lake America’ Order

Google began displaying “Lake America” in place of “Lake Ontario” for U.S. users of Google Maps on Saturday, complying with an executive order President Donald Trump signed Thursday amid an escalating trade dispute with Canada. The order directs the Interior Department to update the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the federal database that governs official American map labels. Google stated its maps are updated “to reflect name changes in official government sources,” and that the change follows the company’s “long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.” Under the new display rules, U.S. users see “Lake America,” Canadian users continue to see “Lake Ontario,” and users elsewhere see both names, with “Lake America” appearing in parentheses.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded by erecting a large sign along the Canadian shoreline reading “Lake Ontario — Now and Always,” criticizing Trump’s move. Ford stated the name would endure beyond the political moment, saying, “Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also rejected the rebranding, writing that “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.” The lake, the smallest of the Great Lakes, sits on the border between New York and Ontario, with its surface area split roughly 52% Canada and 48% U.S.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that MapQuest said it won’t adopt the new name at all, instead rolling out a tool letting users rename the lake to whatever they choose. UPI and CBS News do not mention this detail. Straight Arrow News and Newsweek include information about the Seneca Nation leader criticizing Trump’s decision, while The Daily Wire and BBC attribute the statement to J. Conrad Seneca. UPI and CBS News mention the 50% tariffs imposed by the U.S. on Canadian goods, while The Daily Wire and BBC note that Canada will implement “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs. The Daily Wire and BBC mention Trump’s AI-generated videos, which other accounts do not.

Sources The Daily Wire · UPI · Straight Arrow News · CBS News · Newsweek · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

US, Venezuela tout ‘biggest oil deal in world history’

President Donald Trump announced a sweeping oil agreement with Venezuela, calling it the "biggest oil deal in world history." According to Trump, the deal would give the U.S. majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez praised the agreement, calling it a "historic milestone" and stating it would bring "a significant flow of investment" for Venezuela’s hydrocarbons industry. The deal is expected to develop 17 strategic oil fields, with a production target of more than 1.5 million barrels per day over 25 years. Trump claimed the agreement would "substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future."

The agreement, negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, is said to involve private business interests. A U.S. official told The Associated Press that the U.S. would have a 55% effective interest in the output of a new private company managing the reserves. The deal comes amid high global oil prices and a depleted U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has fallen below 300 million barrels, its lowest level in over four decades.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News claims the deal "MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves," a statement not found in any other account. Fox Business reports the deal targets 1.5 million barrels per day and could generate $200 billion in revenue for Venezuela, while UPI and Washington Examiner mention the U.S. will use Venezuelan oil to "fill up" the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. NPR notes that the U.S. does not have a national oil company and questions how the deal will operate. Fox News states the U.S. will have a 55% effective interest in the output of a new private company, a detail not mentioned in Straight Arrow News or UPI.

Sources Straight Arrow News · Fox Business · UPI · Washington Examiner · FOX News · NPR

El-Sayed apologizes for comments responding to attack on Michigan synagogue

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, apologized to the state's Jewish Democratic Caucus on Saturday for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March. El-Sayed tied the attack to Israel's actions in the Middle East and said his comments may have been misconstrued to justify the attacker's actions. He expressed regret for any pain his remarks may have caused and emphasized that the attack was condemned outright. The synagogue attack occurred in March when a man rammed his car into the building and opened fire on a security guard before dying by suicide. The attacker, Ayman Mohammad Ghazali, had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week prior.

El-Sayed faced criticism for his statement that "hurt people hurt people," which some argued appeared to contextualize or excuse the attacker's actions. He acknowledged that he should have stopped after condemning the attack and admitted that offering context was not the right approach at the time. El-Sayed's apology was part of his effort to unify Democrats after a contentious primary and to move past controversies involving allegations of antisemitism, including his association with Hasan Piker. The Senate race is seen as a key contest for control of the Senate following the 2026 midterms.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and CBS News both report that El-Sayed apologized for comments he made after the synagogue attack, which he tied to Israel's actions. Newsweek adds that the apology comes amid new polling suggesting the Senate race remains competitive and includes details about the FBI's involvement in the attack, noting that Ghazali was inspired by Hezbollah. Washington Examiner states that El-Sayed was criticized for linking Ghazali's actions to military tensions between Israel and Lebanon and includes a quote from El-Sayed about "hurt people hurt people." FOX News focuses on El-Sayed's campaign ties to Hasan Piker and shared donors with Dan Bilzerian, omitting details about the synagogue attack and El-Sayed's apology. Axios provides a detailed account of El-Sayed's apology and his refusal to distance himself from Piker, including quotes from El-Sayed and references to Piker's controversial remarks.

Sources ABC News · CBS News · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · FOX News · Axios

One person killed, five wounded in shooting at rave in Switzerland

A shooting occurred at a rave in Aarau, northern Switzerland, during the early hours of Sunday, leaving one person dead and five others injured. The incident took place at the Schachen horse racing track, where the annual techno party "Aarau Rave VOL. 7" was being held. Police confirmed that a 22-year-old woman died at the scene, while four men and one woman, aged between 24 and 27, were taken to the hospital with injuries ranging from minor to severe. All victims are residents of Switzerland, though Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni identified the deceased as Italian citizen Maria Spinelli and noted that two other injured individuals were also Italian. A large-scale police operation is ongoing to locate the perpetrators, who remain unknown.

Authorities were alerted to the shooting around 2:30 a.m. local time, with witnesses initially mistaking the sounds for fireworks. The shooting occurred during the rave, which had attracted approximately 3,500 attendees. Police have not yet determined the motive or exact circumstances of the incident, though they have ruled out the possibility that the suspects pose a threat again. The Swiss government has deployed a significant police presence, including armed officers and an army helicopter, as part of the investigation.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and UPI both mention that the shooting occurred before 3 a.m., while BBC and CBS News specify it was around 2:30 a.m. Al Jazeera and UPI state that the victims were all Swiss residents, whereas Associated Press and CBS News note that two of the injured were Italian citizens, as identified by Giorgia Meloni. UPI and ABC News mention that cartridge casings indicated at least two calibers of ammunition were used, suggesting multiple weapons, while Al Jazeera and BBC do not specify the type of firearms used. Associated Press and CBS News report that the police ruled out a terrorist attack, citing that the rave was already winding down, a claim not explicitly made by Al Jazeera or UPI.

Sources Al Jazeera · Associated Press · ABC News · BBC · UPI · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Russian drone strike near Kyiv kills 37, damages 50 homes

A Russian drone strike hit an ammunition depot near Kyiv on Friday, killing at least 37 people and injuring 42 others, including four children. The attack occurred in the village of Myla, 15 miles outside central Kyiv, and caused widespread destruction, including damage to at least 50 residential buildings and a care home for elderly and disabled people. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the storage of explosives near civilian areas, stating criminal proceedings had been opened for "official negligence." The strike followed similar incidents in recent months, including a July attack on a depot in Vyshneve that killed 22 people. Local officials reported that the attack sparked a fire and explosions that lasted for several hours, with rescue operations ongoing.

Volodymyr, a security guard in Myla, described the aftermath of the strike, noting that the village's garden and home were severely damaged. He and his family, who had no electricity or water after the attack, found some surviving vegetables to share. Vira, 65, and her son Serhii, who hid in a bunker during the attack, blamed those who stored the ammunition in their village. They reported finding a missile shell, several mines, and cluster munitions on their property after the explosions subsided.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that 38 people died in the attack, with four still missing, while NPR and UPI state the death toll is at least 37. The Guardian also mentions that 30 of the dead were from a care home, while BBC and NPR cite 34 from the same facility. UPI and BBC note that a local official, Taras Didych, was killed while helping at the scene, which is not mentioned in the Guardian or NPR accounts. The Guardian and BBC describe the warehouse as storing "explosive objects," while NPR and UPI specify it as an ammunition depot. The Guardian and BBC mention that the warehouse was owned by the Ukrainian military, a detail not included in NPR or UPI reports.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · UPI · Straight Arrow News · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Official asks for assistance preserving bodies as number of deaths in Nepal floods rises

Rescue efforts in Nepal continue after devastating floods, with the death toll rising to 675 and 2,498 people missing, according to Nepal’s Disaster Management Authority. At least seven were killed in Tibet, and 554 are missing. The Independent Power Producers’ Association reported that almost 900 Nepali employees working on hydropower projects are unaccounted for, with 361 rescued. Nepal Electricity Authority stated that at least 12 hydropower projects are out of action due to flooding, and another 15 under construction are affected. Mass burials have started in several districts, but preserving bodies has become difficult. The Nepali foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, requested assistance from foreign governments to obtain freezers for preserving victims’ bodies, citing the risk of fast decomposition due to bodies being in water for a long time. A preliminary assessment by Chinese and Nepalese experts identified the disaster as triggered by the collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. The Chinese Foreign Ministry noted that rising temperatures are accelerating glacier melt in the Himalayas, increasing the risk of collapses and sudden flooding. Khanal also addressed the growing threat from climate change in the Himalayas, speaking with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who agreed to increase the sharing of real-time hydrological data.

Where the accounts differ

Straight Arrow News reports that the death toll rose by more than 50 people over six hours, though there could be more. This detail is not included in the NPR account. Straight Arrow News also mentions that Dr. Sameer Kumar Adhikari, joint spokesperson of the Ministry of Health and Food Hygiene in Nepal, stated that body management has begun in several districts, including Chitwan and East Nawalparasi. NPR does not include this information. Additionally, Straight Arrow News states that teams from India and China arrived in Nepal on Saturday to assist in rescuing workers, a detail not present in the NPR account.

Sources Straight Arrow News · NPR

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Far-right UK provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE in US

Milo Yiannopoulos, a British far-right commentator, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the United States. According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Yiannopoulos overstayed his legal authorization to remain in the US after entering the country through New York City on May 14, 2019. He was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on July 22, after failing to appear for his immigration hearing. Yiannopoulos was arrested at the Louis Armstrong International Airport in New Orleans on Thursday, August 27, 2026, and is currently in ICE custody pending deportation. The DHS stated that he will be removed from the US, with the exact location of his detention unspecified.

Yiannopoulos was in New Orleans for a concert by the musician Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. TMZ was the first to report his detainment. Laura Loomer, a Trump ally, claimed to have reported Yiannopoulos to ICE and FBI after he called for her assassination. Yiannopoulos, who previously supported Donald Trump, has since become a critic of the former president, though he still supports his agenda. He has called for mass deportations and supported ICE raids, including advocating for checkpoints at public places.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both state that Yiannopoulos was detained and is awaiting deportation, but The Guardian adds that his deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, while Al Jazeera does not specify the timing of his deportation. The Guardian also mentions that Yiannopoulos was arrested while heading to a concert by Ye, while Al Jazeera notes that TMZ was the first to report his detainment. UPI states that Yiannopoulos was deported to the UK on the same day as his detention, while CBS News and The Daily Wire do not specify the exact timing of his deportation. The Daily Wire also includes additional details about Yiannopoulos’s past, including his work with Ye and his internships with Marjorie Taylor Greene, which are not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian · CBS News · UPI · The Daily Wire

Trump’s Greenland threats cast a shadow on Iceland’s vote on whether to trigger EU membership talks

Icelanders are voting Saturday on whether to resume negotiations to join the European Union, with U.S. President Donald Trump’s push for U.S. control of neighboring Greenland adding a new security dimension to the debate. The referendum, which asks voters if Iceland should resume accession negotiations with the EU, is seen as a high-stakes decision for the country, which has long been a NATO ally and relies on U.S. defense commitments. If voters reject the proposal, it could delay EU membership talks for a generation. A yes vote would trigger negotiations with the EU’s executive branch, the European Commission, which would involve discussions on 35 areas, including Iceland’s fishing stocks in the North Atlantic. The vote is also framed as a test of Iceland’s independence and its place in the global geopolitical landscape.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and FOX News both mention Trump’s interest in Greenland and its impact on Iceland’s referendum, but FOX News adds that Trump has previously considered using military force to acquire Greenland, a detail absent in the AP account. The Christian Science Monitor and BBC both highlight the importance of fishing rights and sovereignty in the debate, but the BBC provides more specific details about the number of chapters in the EU accession talks and the process required for membership. Al Jazeera and Straight Arrow News both note the close race in the referendum, but Straight Arrow News includes a specific Gallup poll result (51.6% against, 48.4% in favor) that is not mentioned in Al Jazeera’s account. The BBC and Al Jazeera both mention the cost of living and currency issues, but the BBC provides more detailed information on the economic impact of EU membership, including inflation rates and interest rates.

Sources Associated Press · FOX News · Christian Science Monitor · BBC · Al Jazeera · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump's ex-teleprompter operator fined $172K for betting on speeches

Gabriel Perez, a former White House teleprompter operator, was fined $172,000 for using his position to place bets on prediction markets related to President Donald Trump's speeches. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) ordered Perez to return $107,529 in profits and pay a $65,000 penalty. The fine includes a three-year ban on trading. Perez was accused of using his access to speeches before they were delivered to bet on words or phrases Trump might use. The White House had previously warned staff against participating in prediction markets. Perez worked for Trump since 2016 and was earning a $175,000 salary in 2026. He reportedly made bets on more than a dozen speeches, including the State of the Union and a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.

The case highlights the use of insider information in prediction markets, with the CFTC noting that Perez's actions breached his duty of trust and confidence. Kalshi, the prediction market platform, flagged unusual trading activity and referred the case to the CFTC. The White House Management Office had sent a letter to aides in March advising against betting on prediction markets with nonpublic information.

Where the accounts differ

UPI states Perez was ordered to return $107,529 in unlawful trading and pay a $65,000 penalty, totaling $172,529. The Washington Examiner reports the fine as $172,539.02, including $107,539.02 in profits and a $65,000 penalty. CBS News mentions the fine as $172,000, with $107,500 in profits and a $65,000 penalty. The Guardian and BBC report the fine as $172,000, with $107,539.02 in profits and a $65,000 penalty. Fox Business states the fine as nearly $173K, with $107,539 in profits and a $65,000 penalty. The Washington Examiner and The Guardian attribute the reduction in penalty to Perez's "exemplary cooperation," while UPI and CBS News do not mention this. The Guardian and BBC note that the CFTC thanked Kalshi for its assistance, which is not mentioned in UPI, CBS News, or Fox Business.

Sources UPI · Washington Examiner · CBS News · The Guardian · BBC · Fox Business

No source labeled right covered this story.

Psychiatrist Who Testified For Prosecution In Lindsay Clancy Trial Appears To Have Been Fired

Dr. Avram Mack, a prosecution rebuttal witness in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, is reported to no longer be employed by Nemours Children’s Health in Delaware. CT Insider reported that as of Friday, Mack was no longer associated with the hospital, and Nemours later confirmed he resigned on Monday. Mack, a child and adolescent psychiatrist, testified that Clancy showed no signs of psychosis and that some of her fears were normal for a new mother. He also disputed the duration of the postpartum period, arguing it should be limited to four weeks. The prosecution closed its case by asserting that Clancy acted intentionally and rationally when she killed her children. The jury is expected to resume deliberations on Monday.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller both report that Mack is no longer employed by Nemours Children’s Health, with The Daily Wire noting that a directory search for his name on the hospital’s website came up empty. The Daily Caller adds that a patient reported being informed that all of Mack’s patients were being moved to new providers. The Federalist and Washington Examiner do not mention Mack’s employment status, focusing instead on the trial’s broader implications. The Daily Wire also notes that Mack’s resume stated he had been employed at Nemours since 2023, while The Daily Caller cites his LinkedIn profile for that information. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller both report that Mack testified Clancy described hearing a “loud male voice” instructing her to kill her children, a detail not included in the other accounts.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Federalist · FOX News · Washington Examiner

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Trump Calls For Ranchers And Farmers To ‘Process Their Own Food’

President Donald Trump announced Friday that ranchers and farmers will be given the right to process their own food, calling the current meat processing industry a “nasty Monopoly.” The White House cited the top-four food processors in the U.S.—JBS USA, Tyson Foods, Cargill, and National Beef Packing Company—as holding 80% to 85% of the beef processing business. Trump claimed these companies have “squeezed America’s cattle producers, shrunk herds, and jacked up prices at the grocery store.” The move was framed as an effort to break up the monopoly and support farmers.

Ranchers and industry analysts expressed mixed reactions to the proposal. Some, like MAHA advocate Shawn Hendrix, praised the plan as a necessary step to challenge the meatpacking industry. Others, such as Kansas cattle producer Mike Schultz, acknowledged that while independent processing could offer an alternative, it would not solve all the economic challenges facing ranchers. Schultz and livestock-market analyst John Nalivka emphasized that larger processors benefit from economies of scale, making it difficult for smaller facilities to compete.

The Guardian reported that Trump’s plan comes amid backlash from the U.S. agricultural sector over his decision to pause tariffs on foreign beef. Trump’s agriculture secretary, Brooke Rollins, described the move as a “matter of national security,” stating the U.S. must be able to “feed and fuel ourselves.” However, the administration’s authority to enact these changes remains unclear, as a bill to ease USDA inspections for small ranches is stalled in Congress.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Guardian both describe Trump’s announcement and the White House’s claim that meat processors have squeezed farmers, but only The Daily Wire names the four major processors and specifies their market share. The Guardian does not name the processors or mention their market share. The Daily Caller reports that ranchers are skeptical about the plan’s effectiveness, noting that smaller processors face economic and regulatory hurdles, a detail absent in the other accounts. The Guardian also mentions the context of Trump’s decision to pause tariffs on foreign beef, which is not included in the other accounts.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Seneca Nation leader urges Trump to rescind renaming of Lake Ontario

President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, citing its importance to American history and commerce. The leader of the Seneca Nation, J. Conrad Seneca, criticized the move, calling it "unpresidential" and urging Trump to rescind the order. Seneca argued that the lake's name originates from Indigenous peoples and should remain as it is. Ontario Premier Doug Ford also responded to the renaming by erecting a large sign along the Canadian shoreline stating "Lake Ontario - Now and Always," emphasizing the lake's historical name.

The White House defended the renaming, stating that the majority of the lake's volume lies within U.S. territory and that the name change reflects American heritage. The U.S. Geological Survey officially designated the lake as Lake America in its electronic documents, though the change does not require Canada or private companies to adopt the new name. The move has sparked a trade dispute between the U.S. and Canada, with both nations imposing retaliatory tariffs on each other's goods.

Where the accounts differ

UPI reports that Jérôme Marty, executive director at the International Association for Great Lakes Research, stated the lake was named by Indigenous people and that the name was used to name the province of Ontario. FOX News includes a quote from Seneca referencing Article 6 of the U.S. Constitution, which is not present in UPI. CBS News and BBC both mention the Seneca Nation leader's criticism of the order violating a treaty, while UPI does not mention a specific treaty. Newsweek and BBC note that the name Ontario comes from the Iroquoian word "oniatarí:io," while UPI refers to the name as coming from Indigenous people without specifying the language. FOX News includes a quote from Seneca about President George Washington signing a treaty with the Seneca in 1794, which is not in UPI or CBS News.

Sources UPI · FOX News · Newsweek · CBS News · BBC

Abdul el Sayed apologizes to Michigan Jews for controversial synagogue attack statement

Abdul el Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, apologized to the state's Jewish Democratic Caucus for comments he made following a March attack on a synagogue. El Sayed acknowledged that his remarks, which linked the attack to Israel's actions in the Middle East, may have been misinterpreted. He stated, “My comments may have been misconstrued to justify something I did not mean to justify,” and expressed regret for any pain his words may have caused. The attack occurred when Ayman Mohammad Ghazali, a man who had lost relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon, drove his vehicle into the Temple Israel synagogue in Detroit, killing a security guard before taking his own life. The FBI described the attack as a “targeted act of violence” and a “Hezbollah-inspired act of terrorism.”

El Sayed faced criticism for his statement that “hurt people hurt people,” which some argued appeared to justify Ghazali’s actions. He later clarified that his intent was to provide context for the attacker’s motivations, not to excuse the violence. El Sayed also reportedly told attendees, “no one deserves to have their pain trampled on.” His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, accused him of failing to adequately apologize and of surrounding himself with “terrorist sympathizers.”

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner reports that El Sayed made his apology at an event hosted by the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus and that he said, “If my statement caused pain, I’m sorry. That’s not what I intended.” It also states that the FBI called the attack a “targeted act of violence” and that no one was hurt in the incident, including children in the synagogue’s early childhood program. The Washington Examiner also includes details about El Sayed’s medical background and his comments about his psychiatry rotation. The other accounts do not mention these specifics.

Dolly Parton’s Legacy Under Fire as Left Claims Her as Socialist Mascot

Dolly Parton, the iconic country singer and philanthropist, died at 80, sparking widespread mourning. Throughout her career, she consistently avoided becoming a political figure, rejecting attempts by media and politicians to label her as partisan. She declined the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times, once under President Trump and twice under Biden, to avoid misinterpretation of her political views. Parton was also known for her Imagination Library, a program that sent free books to children from birth to age five, which she launched in 1995 to promote literacy.

Despite her clear stance against politics, major left-wing figures quickly claimed her as a socialist after her death, despite her public record of nonpartisanship. This has led to criticism that they are distorting her legacy. Parton’s comments on race, often cited by left-wing outlets as evidence of her political leanings, were presented in a broader context that suggests she did not intend to make political statements.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire claims that left-wing outlets have misrepresented Dolly Parton’s political views, particularly regarding her comments on race, which it says were taken out of context. The Daily Wire attributes these claims to outlets like NPR, BBC, and The Guardian. The Daily Wire states that these outlets have selectively quoted Dolly Parton’s comments on black lives to signal political allegiance, despite her clear intention to avoid political statements. The other accounts do not mention this specific context or the alleged misrepresentation of her comments.

Sources The Daily Wire · NPR · The Dispatch · BBC · The Guardian · Al Jazeera

Trump announces ‘biggest oil deal in world history’ with Venezuela

President Donald Trump announced a major oil deal with Venezuela, claiming it secures majority U.S. control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves. The agreement, described as "the biggest oil deal in world history," is expected to lower gas prices for Americans. Trump stated the deal was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth with Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez and private businesses. Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez welcomed the deal, stating it would "have a significant impact on our nation's revival." The agreement is expected to bring nearly $100 billion in private investment and over $209 billion in tax revenue to Venezuela.

The deal is part of Trump’s efforts to revive Venezuela’s oil industry, which has been in decline due to years of mismanagement and sanctions. Trump claimed the agreement would "substantially lower" gas prices for Americans "long into the future." The U.S. government would retain 55% control of a joint venture with an "experienced private operator in Venezuela," according to a U.S. official. The agreement also calls for the development of 17 strategic oil fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and ABC News both report that the deal would bring nearly $100 billion in private investment to Venezuela, while The Daily Wire and Washington Examiner mention the same figure. BBC and The New York Post state the deal would bring over $209 billion in tax revenue to Venezuela, which is not mentioned in Al Jazeera or ABC News. The Washington Examiner and The New York Post note that Venezuela holds 303 billion barrels of oil reserves, while Al Jazeera and ABC News refer to 65 billion barrels as the amount under the deal. The Daily Wire and The New York Post mention that the 65 billion barrels represent a substantial portion of Venezuela’s known reserves, which is not stated in other accounts. The Washington Examiner and The New York Post also note that the deal involves fields previously controlled by former Venezuelan insiders, including some indicted by the Justice Department, which is not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources Al Jazeera · ABC News · BBC · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Daily Wire

Six months into the Iran war, a new Gulf security architecture is emerging

The war with Iran has prompted Gulf states to rethink their security strategies, moving toward a more integrated and layered defense system. The conflict has exposed vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure and highlighted the need for stronger regional cooperation. Gulf states are now deepening partnerships with a broader range of allies, including Turkey and European nations, while maintaining their reliance on the United States for security. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan exemplifies this shift, extending collective defense commitments beyond the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).

The war has also accelerated the development of a more flexible security framework, moving away from a single, hierarchical alliance model toward overlapping partnerships. This approach allows for tailored responses to different threats, with varying degrees of regional and international involvement. While the U.S. remains a key player, Gulf states are increasingly taking the lead in shaping their own security arrangements, reflecting a broader trend toward regional autonomy and cooperation.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that the Gulf is moving toward a "layered security system" with stronger cooperation among Gulf states and deeper relationships with Turkey, European states, and other partners. Axios focuses on Trump's evolving strategies for ending the war, including military objectives, economic pressure, and diplomatic efforts. Washington Examiner highlights the U.S. Treasury's role in economic sanctions against Iran's trading partners, particularly China and Turkey. The Guardian emphasizes the financial strain on the U.S. Navy due to the war, while Newsweek outlines potential future scenarios for the conflict. BBC provides a general overview of Trump's accomplishments and the ongoing nature of the war.

Sources Al Jazeera · Axios · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · Newsweek · BBC

Far-right UK provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE in US

Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right British commentator, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport on August 27, 2026. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) stated that Yiannopoulos legally entered the US through New York City on May 14, 2019, but overstayed his visa. An immigration judge issued him a final order of removal on July 22 after he failed to appear for his immigration hearing. Yiannopoulos will remain in ICE custody pending deportation. The DHS also posted a photo that appeared to be a mugshot of Yiannopoulos, warning that those detained for overstaying their visit would be "arrested and deported without a chance to return." Laura Loomer, a Trump ally, claimed credit for Yiannopoulos’s detainment, stating she reported him to ICE and FBI after he called for her assassination.

Yiannopoulos, known for his anti-Islamic postings and online trolling, was previously banned by Twitter in 2016 for inflammatory content. His account was reinstated under Elon Musk’s leadership. He founded a talent management company in Los Angeles and has worked with figures like Kanye West and Marjorie Taylor Greene. The DHS cited his call to "deport millions and millions of people" in June 2025 as part of his rhetoric.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both state Yiannopoulos was detained at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport, while The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire specify the location as Kenner, Louisiana. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention Yiannopoulos was listed in ICE’s online detainee database as being in "ICE Custody," while Al Jazeera and The Daily Caller do not specify the detention facility. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note Yiannopoulos was an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene in 2022, while The Daily Caller and The Guardian refer to him as an unpaid summer intern. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention Yiannopoulos was in Louisiana for a Kanye West concert, while The Daily Caller and The Guardian do not specify the reason for his presence.

Sources Al Jazeera · BBC · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Guardian · Just The News

Fed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persists

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh emphasized in his first major speech that the Fed’s primary responsibility is to achieve stable prices, despite persistent inflation. He did not specify when interest rates might rise, but markets interpreted his remarks as a signal that rate hikes could be coming in September. Warsh described the labor market as reasonably strong and noted that inflation had not yet been tamed. His speech, delivered at the Jackson Hole symposium, marked a shift from previous Fed practices of providing forward guidance. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, intervened in bond markets to lower long-term interest rates, a move that contrasted with Warsh’s more restrained approach. Both officials face criticism for their differing strategies, with Warsh’s focus on short-term rates and Bessent’s on long-term rates.

Where the accounts differ

The Christian Science Monitor reports that Warsh’s speech led to minimal movement in Treasury bond yields, while the Guardian notes that yields on two-year and 10-year notes increased slightly after his speech. The Axios account highlights that Warsh has avoided providing forward guidance, a stance also mentioned by the BBC and NPR. The Guardian and BBC both mention that Warsh criticized the use of forward guidance as a legacy of the 2008 financial crisis, while the Christian Science Monitor attributes this critique to Warsh directly. The Fox Business account includes details about Warsh’s discussion of artificial intelligence’s impact on the economy, which is not mentioned in the other accounts. The BBC and NPR both note that Warsh did not offer a detailed roadmap for interest rates, while the Guardian and Axios emphasize the market’s interpretation of his speech as a signal for potential rate hikes.

Sources Christian Science Monitor · The Guardian · Axios · Fox Business · NPR · BBC

Artemis II crew receives Space Medal of Honor as Trump establishes academy

President Donald Trump on Friday bestowed the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on the Artemis II crew, marking their historic achievement during a ceremony at Johnson Space Center in Houston. The crew, consisting of NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, along with Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, traveled farther into deep space than anyone else in history during their trip around the Moon in April. The mission served as a test flight for NASA's plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as early as 2028. Trump also signed an executive order establishing the U.S. Space Academy, a national academy similar to the service academies for the armed forces.

During the ceremony, Trump personally placed the medal around the necks of each astronaut as they were recognized for their work during the mission. The president used the occasion to highlight the importance of the Artemis II mission, stating that it demonstrated the courage and service of the astronauts and their contributions to space exploration. The event also included a presentation of the medals to the crew, with each astronaut expressing gratitude for the recognition and the support they received from their families, NASA, and the international community.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that Trump mentioned a story about being in an important meeting when someone asked to watch the Artemis II mission, and that he had a television set pulled up for the group to watch. CBS News includes a quote from Trump about Sen. Ted Cruz lobbying for Texas as the location of the academy, which UPI also mentions. FOX News states that the Artemis II crew traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before, a detail not included in ABC News. The Daily Wire includes a quote from Trump about planting a flag on the Moon before the end of his term, which is not mentioned in other accounts. Just The News provides a more detailed description of the medal's criteria and its historical context, which is not included in ABC News.

Sources ABC News · CBS News · UPI · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

White House silent on Iran-Oman Hormuz plan as CENTCOM claims strait cleared of Iranian mines

The Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil passage, has been the focus of a dispute between the U.S. and Iran. Iran and Oman proposed a framework to reopen the strait, which Tehran claims would exclude military vessels. The White House did not comment on whether President Trump would accept any restrictions on U.S. warships under the arrangement. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins stated that the strait is an international waterway where commercial vessels continue to transit with U.S. military assistance.

CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper announced that the strait's international shipping lanes are free of Iranian sea mines, calling it a "major milestone." He credited the U.S. military for clearing the mines under dangerous conditions. Cooper also stated that no ships have entered or left Iranian ports without U.S. permission, and that ships have only been allowed to pass through on humanitarian grounds. According to U.S. officials, the number of ships transiting the strait has increased, though it remains below pre-war levels.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi refuted claims that the strait is open, stating that no vessels have transited without Iran's permission. He accused the U.S. of making propaganda to calm global energy markets. Meanwhile, the White House remained silent on the Iran-Oman proposal, with no response to questions about Trump's potential acceptance of restrictions on U.S. military vessels.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the White House did not respond to questions about Trump's potential acceptance of restrictions on U.S. warships under the Iran-Oman proposal. It also mentions that the Trump administration has applied military and economic pressure to reopen the strait on U.S. terms, with oil flows at about 5 million barrels per day. New York Post and UPI both state that CENTCOM claims the strait is cleared of Iranian mines, while Axios adds that U.S. officials say only 11 of the 200 mine-like objects swept from the strait were actual mines. FOX News also notes that the White House did not comment on the Iran-Oman plan, while Axios and UPI mention Trump's public claims about the strait being open.

Sources FOX News · New York Post · Axios · UPI

Trump’s Greenland threats cast a shadow on Iceland’s vote on whether to trigger EU membership talks

Icelanders are voting Saturday on whether to resume long-stalled negotiations to join the European Union, with the referendum taking place amid concerns over U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to control Greenland. The vote, which is expected to be close, will determine whether Iceland will begin the process of becoming a full EU member. If voters reject the proposal, the issue will be put on hold for at least a generation. A yes vote would trigger negotiations with the EU’s executive branch, the European Commission, which would involve discussions on 35 areas, including Iceland’s fishing stocks in the North Atlantic. The referendum is seen by some as a way to secure additional security guarantees against potential U.S. expansionism in the region.

Trump’s comments about acquiring Greenland have raised concerns in Iceland, which is just 180 miles away from the self-governing territory of Denmark, a longtime U.S. ally. While Trump has not indicated he will use force to seize Greenland, his interest in the territory has not waned. Icelanders fear that if Greenland is seized, Iceland could be next. The referendum is also framed as a way to gain protection from potential U.S. encroachment, with some believing the EU could offer such safeguards.

Where the accounts differ

The Associated Press and the Washington Examiner both report that Trump’s threats to Greenland have influenced Iceland’s referendum, but the Washington Examiner includes a direct quote from Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, which the Associated Press omits. The Straight Arrow News and the Christian Science Monitor differ in the reported polling numbers, with Straight Arrow News citing Gallup at 51.6% against and 48.4% in favor, while the Christian Science Monitor reports a similar split but attributes it to different sources. The Al Jazeera and BBC accounts differ in the population figures for Iceland, with Al Jazeera stating 395,000 and the BBC stating under 400,000. The BBC also notes that Iceland is one of Europe’s most affluent nations, a claim not made by the other outlets.

Sources Associated Press · Washington Examiner · Straight Arrow News · Christian Science Monitor · Al Jazeera · BBC

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: National Guard's fatal shooting of a man in the back raises urgent questions about lethal force use and accountability in law enforcement.

Tennessee national guard fatally shot armed man in back, autopsy shows

The Tennessee National Guard shot 20-year-old Tyrin Johnson in the back, according to an autopsy report obtained by the Associated Press. The report, shared by Johnson’s family, states a single bullet entered his right side and exited through his upper right chest. This contradicts initial police accounts that said Johnson was shot in the chest after turning toward the guards. Memphis police reported that Johnson was running from officers when he was shot, while the autopsy suggests he was running away from the shooter. The National Guard was part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, created by Donald Trump, and was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.

The autopsy report, conducted by the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center Office of the Medical Examiner, also noted that there was no soot, gunpowder stippling, or muzzle imprint around the wound, indicating Johnson was likely shot from more than three feet away. Dr. Steven White, a forensic pathologist, said this is consistent with Johnson running away from the shooter. Johnson’s family attorney, Andre Wharton, stated that the law enforcement narrative does not match the autopsy findings, calling it a "blatant inconsistency."

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the autopsy findings, obtained by the Associated Press, were shared by Johnson’s family and include an "investigative narrative" from a Tennessee Bureau of Investigation agent stating Johnson was turning toward law enforcement with a gun. The report also mentions that the National Guard responded to a police call and that both guards fired their weapons. The BBC notes that the TBI did not distribute the claim that Johnson turned and pointed a gun at the guards, and that the report includes a separate statement about Johnson carrying a "handgun magazine with rounds." The Guardian also mentions that the National Guard report said two guards responded to the call and approached the suspect, who "rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them."

Sources The Guardian · BBC
